summary: Considers what IPv6 support cellular hosts need on GPRS, UMTS and EPS networks, given the limits of cellular links in bandwidth, cost and delay. It is guidance for implementers.

plainLanguage.summary: It lists which parts of the new internet addressing system a phone needs and which it can skip.

questions: does a cellular host need duplicate address detection
subtitle: Which IPv6 features a phone or cellular modem should implement, and which it can safely skip, on 3GPP networks.

tldr.problem: IPv6 is a large set of specifications, and cellular links differ from ordinary links in bandwidth, cost and delay, so implementers need guidance on what a cellular host should do.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC goes through the IPv6 node requirements and notes where a host on GPRS, UMTS or EPS networks needs clarification, such as Neighbor Discovery, address autoconfiguration, DHCPv6, router options and extension headers.
tldr.outcome: It is informational guidance on top of the IPv6 Node Requirements, not a new protocol, and it obsoletes RFC 3316.

today: RFC 7066 is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 3316. It has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Scope and Audience
sections.content:
This document covers IPv6 for cellular hosts that attach to GPRS, UMTS or EPS networks, collectively called 3GPP networks. It complements the IPv6 Node Requirements in RFC 6434 where clarification is needed, and it is written from the point of view of the host.

It is informational. It is not meant to replace, update or contradict any IPv6 standard, and it is aimed at implementers. Transition mechanisms are out of scope, although the primary one supported by 3GPP is dual-stack (RFC 4213). Mobility is also treated as not relevant here, since movement inside 3GPP networks is mostly handled by link-layer mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: This guide is for people who build phones and modems. It adds notes to the general IPv6 rulebook for the special case of cellular links.

sections.title: Neighbor Discovery on a Cellular Link
sections.content:
GPRS, UMTS and EPS links resemble a point-to-point link, so the host's only neighbor is its default router, which it already knows from Router Discovery. There are no link-layer addresses on the 3GPP cellular link, so address resolution and next-hop determination are not needed. The host must still support Neighbor Solicitation and Advertisement and Neighbor Unreachability Detection (RFC 4861), and it always solicits for routers when the interface comes up.

To limit periodic signaling, upper layers should give reachability confirmations where possible. TCP can do this. For UDP-based traffic the RFC suggests using the DNS response, RTCP feedback for RTP, and responses to SIP requests as the confirmation.
sections.plainLanguage: On a cellular link there is only one other device to talk to, like a walkie-talkie with two people, so the phone does not need a big address book. It can use replies it already gets as proof the other side is there.

sections.title: Addresses and Autoconfiguration
sections.content:
Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (RFC 4862) is the only mandatory way to configure an IPv6 address in a 3GPP cellular host. The Router Advertisement carries at most one prefix information option with infinite valid and preferred lifetimes, the prefix can never be used for on-link determination, and its lifetime is tied to the PDP Context or PDN Connection. The host does not need special handling for this.

Hosts can set DupAddrDetectTransmits to zero, because each assigned prefix is unique within its scope. The GGSN/PGW supplies the interface identifier that must be used for the link-local address, so duplicate address detection is not required there either. Where PPP is used between the mobile terminal and the terminal equipment, the host must support the IPV6CP interface identifier option and the MT must reject interface identifiers suggested by the TE.

DHCPv6 is neither required nor supported for address autoconfiguration as of 3GPP Release-11, but Stateless DHCPv6 and Prefix Delegation may be used for other configuration needs. Privacy extensions (RFC 4941) may be supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone network hands out the phone's address and a unique name for its end of the link, so the phone does not need to shout to check that nobody else has the same one.

sections.title: Extra Router and Configuration Options
sections.content:
A cellular host should implement a few more options.

  • The Default Router Preferences and More-Specific Routes extension (RFC 4191), useful when the host has other IPv6 interfaces.
  • The Router Advertisement options for DNS configuration (RFC 6106), because DNS servers are otherwise learned from link-layer signaling, which can be cumbersome when the MT and TE are separated.
  • The Prefix Exclude Option for DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation (RFC 6603). Prefix Delegation was added as optional in Release-10, and the /64 prefix on the 3GPP link must aggregate with the shorter delegated prefix.
  • The MTU option in Router Advertisements. The 3GPP packet core uses extensive tunneling, so the GGSN/PGW may propose an MTU that accounts for the overhead.

Sending MLD reports for link-local addresses is not necessary on these point-to-point links, though it does no harm.
sections.plainLanguage: A few extra settings are worth having, like the right size for packets, since the network wraps them in extra envelopes on the way through.

sections.title: Security and Extension Headers
sections.content:
IPsec is a fundamental but not mandatory part of IPv6, and the security requirements of RFC 6434 also apply. By default the host should follow the RH0 handling in RFC 5095, since Routing Header Type 0 is deprecated. It must follow the handling of overlapping fragments in RFC 5722 and must not fragment Neighbor Discovery messages (RFC 6980).

The security discussion notes that the RFC introduces no new protocols or vulnerabilities. In the 3GPP model hosts do not use device-unique interface identifiers, so the network prefix is the only part of the address that differs, which already gives a limited form of addressing privacy. Because airtime is expensive and capacity limited, denial-of-service attacks such as packet amplification can be more damaging in the cellular environment. Local interfaces such as WLAN or Bluetooth should have access control so others cannot use the host as an intermediary.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone connections cost money and are easy to clog, so a phone should refuse odd or dangerous kinds of packets and keep its other doors, like Wi-Fi, locked.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3316
sections.content: This document replaces RFC 3316. Among the listed changes, sections that can be found directly in RFC 6434 were removed, and new material was added: Evolved Packet System text, clarifications on how Neighbor Discovery works on the 3GPP link, DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation recommendations, Router Advertisement MTU option handling, and recommendations based on RFC 4191 and RFC 6106. It also clarifies that DHCPv6 is not used at all for address autoconfiguration, and adds references on the RH0 deprecation and fragment handling.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the updated version of an older checklist, with the parts that now live in the main rulebook removed and new phone-network features added.
